corpora.title: Upstream FFmpeg spatial defects that cross the MALLOC BOUND, FFmpeg's not-nested row
corpora.note: The third plain-heap corpus, after memcached's and wireshark's, and a sibling of subobject-repros and pool-repros rather than part of either: those boundaries are 'inside one allocation' and 'storage an AVBufferPool handed out', while every case here leaves a buffer FFmpeg obtained DIRECTLY from av_malloc_array or av_calloc. Under this inventory's axis (WHO ALLOCATED THE OBJECT) all four rows are NOT NESTED. ASan REPORTS all four, two-sided, unlike the sub-object corpora -- which is the contrast this corpus exists to draw. Case 2 is the only row in the whole inventory that crosses BELOW an allocation's base. All four are fix-reversals: liveness is recorded, never required, and requiring it is what kept FFmpeg's spatial count at four. WHY THE PLATFORM ALLOCATOR. These cases call the platform's calloc, not the buffer-pool port's av_malloc. That port's av_malloc (ports/ffmpeg/buffer-pool/src/shared/metadata-allocator.c:26) is a bump/freelist carve out of ONE arena returning a raw interior pointer, and it rounds every request up to 64 bytes; __builtin_capstone_cap_shrink appears only in src/capstone-domain/payload-capabilities.c:57, on pool PAYLOAD blocks. Routing these cases through it would leave no per-allocation bound to cross AND would absorb every small crossing in the round-up, so the reading would be about the arena, not the defect. Triage and the full candidate disposition: docs/ref/ffmpeg-spatial-defect-triage.md. CheriBSD MEASURED 2026-10-06 (results/20261006-cheribsd): 3 of 4 CAUGHT with the fault attributed to the labelled probe, si_code 1; case 1 NOT caught, refuting its pre-registered prediction because its 24-byte request yields a 32-byte capability. This is the first CheriBSD reading of any FFmpeg corpus, and the first in the tree where attribution is established -- the probes are defined once externally rather than static per translation unit.

corpora.title: Eleven spatial and temporal defects live in Perl 5.36.3, each measured live at the pin and clean at master, with what each arm sees
corpora.live_in_pin_note: Liveness is measured in both directions for every case, not inferred: each trigger reports under ASan on a build of the pin's own tree and is silent on the same trigger, same harness and same ASan options on master. The dates alone would not settle it -- four of the eleven fixes are DATED BEFORE the v5.36.3 tag (2023-11-28) and are still absent from it, because they landed on blead and were never backported to the 5.36 maintenance branch. Each case therefore records the ancestry that was actually checked with git merge-base --is-ancestor, in both directions.
corpora.note: The population was every commit from v5.36.3 to the master tip that touches both C source and a test (457 of 9537), filtered to the ones whose diff has the shape of a spatial or temporal memory defect and triaged by hand against the pin's sources. All eleven cases here are in scope by construction: this corpus admits only spatial and temporal memory defects, which is the study's scope, so unlike the mruby corpus it carries no null dereferences, type confusions or stack-exhaustion rows. One of the eleven is outside every arm's denominator and says so in its own file: 9e298ab597's trigger passes its own assertion on all four Capstone arms and on CheriBSD with revocation off and on, so the stale slot it needs never exists there; host ASan reports SEGV, so the defect is real but the trigger does not travel. The honest denominator is 10. 254b30e378 carried harness_limit until 2026-10-06 and that is WITHDRAWN: the defect did not execute in a domain because perl-cross installs almost none of the target library (636 pure-Perl modules absent, XSLoader.pm among them), so PerlIO_find_layer("scalar") could not require PerlIO::scalar and the open silently took the generic perlio layer. With the library staged by build-perl-domain.sh the case is caught. sysalloc-bounds is the baseline: per-object heap bounds are what applications get by default since PR #170, so a catch is a case the bounds arm does not fault on. The nested-allocator arm is sublet-svheads, and it protects ONE of Perl's nested allocators -- the SV head arena. The SV bodies, hash entries and OP slabs keep their upstream allocators, so a case whose stale pointer lives in those is out of that arm's reach by construction and its arm entry says so. FOUR arms, cumulative, each step adding exactly one thing: sysalloc-bounds is the base an application gets today (per-object heap bounds, no revocation); sysalloc-sublet protects the SYSTEM allocator spatially and temporally (the Sublet heap: bounded, every free revokes); sublet-svheads is that SAME image plus the SV head arena through the lifetime adapter, which makes it this port's analogue of the mruby port's sublet-gc; cheribsd-revocation is the same release on CheriBSD with revocation as it comes. 6, 7, 8, with CheriBSD at 7. sysalloc-sublet is the FLOOR, and it is the right floor because it catches EXACTLY the same seven cases as cheribsd-revocation -- the same set, not merely the same count, with no case unique to either. Once the system allocator is protected as well as CheriBSD protects it, the only thing left to gain is the nested allocator, and it gains exactly one case. The third arm's extra case is 17535c984a, whose SV head never returns to malloc -- invisible to ASan, to a protected system allocator, and to CheriBSD alike, which is the whole argument for protecting a nested allocator. An unprotected variant (CAPSTONE_LEVEL0_OBJECT_BOUNDS=0) was also measured and is recorded in the results bundle as context rather than as an arm: it catches 6 as well, and differs only in reporting the spatial case as an untagged dereference instead of a bounds violation. CheriBSD's revocation is selected per process because the system-wide default kills the guest's own sshd, and every case ran under both settings so the pair controls the knob. The extra case is NOT a quarantine-timing effect: CheriBSD's shadow bitmap, read in O(1) without a sweep, shows all 2983 frees of that run quarantined and zero mallocs returning memory whose bit was still set, so the SV head never crosses the allocator boundary at all. An every-free run does make it SIGPROT and is rejected as evidence, because every-free faults on all eleven including an in-bounds read of a live object that nothing may catch.

corpora.boundary: C reductions that drive the real upstream function, compiled verbatim from the 17.5 pin, with no server in the process
corpora.title: Memory-safety defects in PostgreSQL 17.5 reduced to C against the real upstream function
corpora.note: The counterpart to sql-repros and mmgr-repros, and the reason it exists: both of those are palloc clients, so every defect in them is nested by construction. PostgreSQL's client side is not -- libpq, psql, pg_dump and fe_utils call malloc, realloc and free directly, about 990 call sites against the backend's 82 -- so a defect here is a libc client and is non-nested. Without this corpus the study has no non-nested arm to compare against, and a mechanism's silence on a nested defect cannot be attributed to the nesting. These cases are C reductions, not SQL: the defect is in the client process and no statement sent to a server can reach it. Each drives the real upstream function with a constructed input, the way mmgr-repros drives the real aset and slab. That also makes them freestanding domains, so unlike sql-repros they need no application VM. All five were reproduced on the host under ASan on 2026-10-06 against shared/corpus.h and shared/driver.c, each driving the real upstream function copied verbatim from the pin (shared/upstream_libpq.c, upstream_pgdump.c, upstream_ecpg.c, upstream_saslprep.c, upstream_bbstreamer.c). Each case's host-asan oracle records the faulting access, its size and the exact size of the region it ran off, so the reduction is checkable against the arithmetic in its live_proof rather than taken on trust. RESULT ON THE PURECAP ARM, 2026-10-06: 3 of 5 detected (00, 02, 04 all SIGPROT with their PG_DEFECT marker printed first), 2 reached-silent (01, 03). Every one of the five verdicts is predicted by one measured fact, and the fact is worth more than the ratio: this guest's malloc rounds capability bounds to a SIZE CLASS, not to the request. Measured requested->granted pairs: 1->16, 4->16, 8->16, 16->16, 24->32, 32->32, 100->112, 400->448, 4096->4096. Lining the cases up against it: 00 writes 4096 bytes into an 8-byte request (cap 16) and faults; 02 walks ~4 GiB from a 1-byte request (cap 16) and faults; 04 reads 24 bytes from offset 24 of a 24-byte request (cap 32) and crosses at offset 32, so it faults; 01 reads offset 400 of a 400-byte request (cap 448) and does not; 03 reads offset 4 of a 4-byte request (cap 16) and does not. So a malloc-granular capability machine sees an overrun exactly when it exceeds the ALLOCATOR'S ROUNDING, not when it exceeds the object. Two of five real CVE-class defects are invisible here for that reason alone, with no nesting involved at all -- which is a second blind spot, independent of the one this corpus was built to measure, and it narrows the claim that non-nested defects are the ones such a mechanism catches. On fault attribution: these cases cannot use mmgr-repros' .globl label on the faulting instruction, because in three of the five that instruction is inside a function copied verbatim from upstream and a label would make the copy no longer verbatim. The handler in shared/driver.c reports the faulting PC and the return address as offsets from a function the case names instead, which attributes the fault without touching upstream code; case 00 is why both are reported, since its fault is inside libc's memcpy and only the return address lands in pqGetnchar. One field is NOT usable here and is recorded so nobody relies on it: on this guest SIGPROT arrives with si_addr equal to the faulting PC, not to the data address -- measured as addr==pc on all three faulting cases -- so the fault address cannot be cross-checked against an object's bounds from siginfo. Renamed from c-repros on 2026-10-06, and the old boundary text -- "libpq and the client tools, which allocate from libc and not from a memory context" -- was wrong and is replaced. libpq has a nested allocator of its own: fe-exec.c:563 pqResultAlloc carves every PGresult's subsidiary storage out of 2048-byte PGRESULT_DATA_BLOCKSIZE blocks it mallocs, and upstream's own comment calls it "our trivial space allocator". So a client-side defect is not non-nested by virtue of being client-side. The five cases here are non-nested because of what each one touches -- a caller's buffer, a pg_dump array, an ecpg host variable, an application password, a pg_basebackup chunk -- and not one of them touches PGresult storage. That is a property of the selection, not of the client side, and a future case on PGresult memory would belong here with allocator_layer set accordingly. CORRECTION, 2026-10-06. This corpus previously recorded that the two Capstone arms could not host these cases, on the grounds that a domain's malloc is itself a nested allocator (the spatial arm) or refuses outright (the sublet arm). That was wrong, and it pointed at the wrong code: both of those files, memory-contexts/src/allocators/spatial/backing-allocator.c and .../sublet/unsupported-allocators.c, belong to the memory-contexts replay study and are linked into neither arm image -- checked by symbol, pg_subpool_refuse is absent from both postgres.dom binaries. What an arm image links is ports/musl-capstone/runtime/level0.c, whose CAPSTONE_LEVEL0_OBJECT_BOUNDS has been on by default since 2026-09-30 and which neither arm overrides; malloc there narrows what it returns to the bytes asked for, and the built binaries carry six shrink instructions inside malloc itself. So a non-nested object has always been hostable on both arms. What was missing was a domain build, and shared/build-domain.sh is now it: 5 of 5 cases build against each arm's SDK. Nothing was relaxed to achieve this, and the sublet arm's refusing malloc, whose job is to catch a PostgreSQL memory manager reaching an unadapted libc path, is not part of this build and is unchanged. A prediction worth recording before the run, because it is falsifiable: the purecap guest rounds bounds to a size class and so missed 01 and 03, while level0 bounds the request exactly, so both should be reported here. If they are not, the difference is not bounds granularity and this note is wrong.

corpora.boundary: memory contexts (aset, slab)
corpora.title: Upstream use-after-free and double-free defects in PostgreSQL's memory managers
corpora.note: The allocator pin is 17.0; the complete single-user backend port is 17.5. 2026-10-05: a cheribsd-revocation arm was added by this project and run on all 8. The corpus had no plain-purecap arm, only the two PoisonCap ones, and PoisonCap is out of scope for the study these results feed; without it these 8 could not be compared with the other PostgreSQL corpora, which all carry that arm. The build path already existed -- cmake/Replay.cmake builds one hosted executable per case under PG_CORPUS_DIR and says 'plain CheriBSD' when PG_POISONCAP is off -- so nothing in the corpus or the port was changed to produce it. One qualification on reading those 8 silences, because it bites elsewhere: the guest's security.cheri.runtime_revocation_every_free_default is 0, so a revocation sweep runs only once a quarantine threshold is crossed, and a short case that frees a handful of objects may never cross one -- a silence can then mean 'no sweep ran yet' rather than 'the mechanism could not see it'. That confound does NOT apply here, and the reason is worth stating: pfree returns a chunk to its context and never returns the block to malloc, so there is no malloc free for a sweep to act on at any threshold. The silence is a property of the nesting, not of when the quarantine happens to flush. Re-pinned from 17.0 to 17.5 on 2026-10-06, and three cases moved to not-live-at-17-5/ because `git merge-base --is-ancestor` shows their upstream fixes are already in REL_17_5: 83ce20d671, 727bc6ac33f6 and 9d5ce4f1a00a. The 17.0 pin was the only one in the PostgreSQL study, and it is what let three already-fixed defects appear in a 17.5 result table. The five that remain all have fixes later than REL_17_5 (2025-05-05): 2025-08-02, 2025-08-30, 2025-10-03, 2025-10-09 and 2026-03-30. COMPARABILITY, recorded 2026-10-06 rather than resolved. This corpus's `spatial` and `sublet` rows were measured on 2026-09-18, before the 17.5 re-pin, and against the memory-contexts replay study's level 0 (ports/postgres/memory-contexts/src/allocators): backing-allocator.c for the unprotected arm and the refusing unsupported-allocators.c for the protected one. The sibling corpora sql-repros and c-repros were measured on 2026-10-06 against the application domain, whose level 0 is ports/musl-capstone/runtime/level0.c with CAPSTONE_LEVEL0_OBJECT_BOUNDS on. The two are different allocators with different bounds behaviour -- the replay one hands out pointers carrying the whole arena's bounds, the application one narrows to the request -- so these five rows may be added to a per-arm total only with that stated. They are not withdrawn: each is a real measurement of its own arm, and the temporal result they carry (sublet 5 of 5 where both others report 0 of 5) does not depend on bounds granularity, because a use-after-free is caught by revocation and not by a bound. Rerunning them against the application domain would make the three corpora directly comparable and has not been done.

corpora.boundary: a running PostgreSQL 17.5 server, reached by SQL; no reduction of any kind stands between the statement and the defect
corpora.title: Memory-safety defects in PostgreSQL 17.5 reached by SQL against a real server
corpora.note: Narrowed 2026-10-05 to the four categories the study measures -- temporal and spatial, each nested or not -- and the 14 cases outside them were removed: 4 integer, 5 invariant, 2 type-confusion, 1 wrong-answer, 1 authz, 1 null-deref. They were real defects, reproduced and measured on all three arms, and they are recoverable from commit 607802a0421e; they are gone from here because they do not exercise an allocator and so say nothing about nesting. Of the five that remain, all five allocate through palloc, so all five are nested clients. Two of them (02, 03) overflow by ~32 KB and ~65 KB and therefore leave the underlying malloc block, which a malloc-granular mechanism can see; the other three stay inside the palloc chunk. One removed case is worth re-collecting rather than replacing: 05_levenshtein carried CVE-2026-15742, whose upstream description is an arbitrary-address WRITE via integer wraparound, but our trigger only reached the wrong-answer path -- the case's own fidelity said 'an integer wraparound with no memory error'. The extension, the scaffolding and the fix commit c4d51b62748f are all in hand; what is missing is a trigger that reaches the write. Sibling of mmgr-repros, which pins 17.0 and reduces memory-manager defects to C programs. Our own constructed demonstrators are not here: they are fixtures, which README.md places under ports/*/security-tests. Renamed from sql-repros on 2026-10-06. The old name said WHERE the code lives, and that reads as a claim about the allocator which does not hold: src/backend has 193 direct libc call sites against 2940 palloc-family ones, and a defect on one of those objects would be non-nested in the backend -- 2aa6be6e64 is exactly that, a double free of an EVP_CIPHER_CTX that came from OpenSSL's allocator. The name now says how the defect is REACHED, which is what actually distinguishes this corpus from its two siblings and is what its results can be read as evidence for. Whether a case is nested is decided per case by allocator_layer, not by which directory it sits in.

corpora.boundary: memsys5, SQLite's own arena allocator, under the engine
corpora.title: Engine-internal memory-safety defects in SQLite 3.22.0, measured against a nested allocator
corpora.note: Sibling of capi-repros, not an extension of it: those 19 rows are pointer-lifetime defects in host BINDINGS over the C API, and that corpus records SQLite's engine-internal defects as out of scope. These 43 are engine-internal. Five further R2 fuzz-diff images (fz01, fz03, fz04, fz05, fz07) are collected and carry a host-ASan signature but no derived trigger, so they are not cases here; deriving them needs the 3.43.1 fuzz corpus re-extracted for db-by-sql pairing. Eight more entries in the collection are diagnostics rather than defects -- five baseline probes and three allocator demonstrators -- and stay in the port. The memsys5 boundary is the point: a sub-allocation is the address arena+i*atom, so it inherits the whole arena's bounds, and both a use-after-free and an overflow that stays inside the arena are in bounds for a capability machine. Narrowed to this study's scope on 2026-10-06: five cases moved to not-in-scope/ because they are neither spatial nor temporal -- two non-terminating loops, one unbounded recursion (the exhausted resource is the C stack), one dereference of the literal address 0x3 and one NULL dereference. The last two were not visible in the shape field, which grouped them under "stale or wild pointer dereference" together with two genuine out-of-bounds reads; they were separated by reading each case. The same line was drawn for PostgreSQL at the reviewer's request, so one rule now holds across the study. What remains is 26 temporal and 12 spatial. The runners list now names the CheriBSD side too, which it did not: the two Capstone arms are driven by corpus322.sh and the two CheriBSD arms by the scripts under ports/sqlite/cheribsd, and only the first was declared. tags.tsv is listed with them because it is what the runners take their case list from -- `ls out/` answers what was built, not what the corpus contains, and the difference is not always visible. Narrowed again on 2026-10-06, 38 to 33: five cases moved to no-binary-verdict/ because on at least one arm they produced neither detected nor not-detected. Three had a probe showing hits=0 on cheribsd-revocation -- the defect site never executed, so the arm had nothing to miss -- and two hung on a Capstone arm, neither completing nor faulting. Scoring any of them as not-detected would credit an arm with a silent miss on code that did not run. The cost is recorded there and is not nothing: 26_2c7a73eaea was the only case whose damage left the memsys5 arena, so Table 1b's "leaves the arena" column now has no measured member.

corpora.boundary: the system allocator itself: one g_malloc, with no inner layer
corpora.title: Upstream wiretap spatial defects that cross the MALLOC BOUND, tshark's not-nested row
corpora.note: A sibling of wmem-repros, deliberately separate: that corpus's boundary is wmem -- a chunk carved from a block the system allocator handed out -- and all eighteen of its cases cross a bound wmem owns. These cross the malloc bound itself, in wiretap, which does not use wmem at all and calls g_malloc directly for its page buffers. The corpus is the mirror of memcached/plain-heap-repros and exists for the same reason: tshark's not-nested spatial row stood empty because the hunt had required its candidates to be live at the pin, which no document asks for. It also carries the one tshark row the chunk port is IRRELEVANT to, which is why sublet-chunks is a required arm here: its prediction is that the port changes nothing, because the object is not a wmem chunk. ASan REPORTS these defects, unlike the wmem and sub-object corpora.

corpora.title: Dissector-side defects in consumers of Wireshark's wmem pools: thirteen temporal, nine spatial
corpora.note: Cases 0-12 are temporal; cases 13-21 are SPATIAL, from the hunt recorded in docs/ref/wireshark-spatial-defect-triage.md. Cases 14 and 15 are the corpus's only rows LIVE at the v4.6.8 pin -- every other row, temporal and spatial alike, is a fix-reversal. Note for anyone reading the spatial rows: every arm of this harness narrows a wmem allocation to its request (wm_narrow(), ports/wireshark/wmem/src/shared/wmem-port-hooks.h:11-15), so a spatial crossing faults on ALL arms and these rows do not discriminate the chunk port. Case 13's run established that by refuting its own prediction. Cases 18-21 added 2026-10-07, all SPATIAL and all nested. 18 (716a200295) is the row that FILLS a cell this inventory recorded as empty: a nested-spatial defect LIVE at the v4.6.8 pin, whose guard cannot fire because the user preference it tests defaults to 0. The leads came from bug-corpora/wireshark/LIVE-CANDIDATES.md and from the class-B candidates docs/ref/wireshark-spatial-defect-triage.md:226-229 named and left unbuilt. Two candidates from those lists were REJECTED rather than built: 1c090e9292 is a STACK buffer overflow, so it has no heap allocator boundary, and d7d1686a95 indexes a static value_string array, which likewise has no allocator. 0939cf989d is the same ETSI DCP defect as case 16 under a different hash.

ports.title: The same Perl release, cross-built for CheriBSD purecap
ports.workload: the 17-section smoke, under both libc revocation switches
ports.note: PERL_CHERI_STATIC=1 links the interpreter statically, which the stock CheriBSD loader requires (dynamically linked it is refused with "Traditional TLS not supported" before main). The static image is then rejected at run time: SIGPROT inside perl_construct, on every invocation including perl -v, while a static purecap C hello and mruby's static purecap binary both run on that same image. So this port cannot yet host a corpus arm; see capstone/bug-corpora/perl/release-differential/results/20261006-cheribsd-blocked. The dynamic image's 17-section smoke passed on the PoisonCap platform, whose own sshd dies on a poison exception during a file copy. No inner SV lifetime adapter here either, which is the other reason Perl is not a measured application in the reuse study.
